claims.text: At high temperatures, in situ formation of a stable, multi-oxide tribofilm is the dominant factor governing the wear resistance of thin FeNiCrCoCu coatings.
The oxide tribofilm reduces direct metal–metal contact.
Reducing direct metal–metal contact slows coating degradation and enhances wear resistance.
The baseline is an unmodified, standard-composition FeNiCrCoCu thin coating on a steel substrate.
Increasing the relative chromium content will promote more robust oxide-tribofilm formation at high temperature.
Increasing another oxygen-affine element could also promote more robust oxide-tribofilm formation.
Continuous, dense oxide layers formed during sliding lower friction.
Continuous, dense oxide layers prevent direct metal–metal contact.
Elevated temperature and sliding shear cause preferential oxidation of the coating surface.
The multi-principal-element nature of FeNiCrCoCu promotes formation of a uniform, thermally stable oxide scale.
A uniform, thermally stable oxide scale reduces abrasive wear.
A uniform, thermally stable oxide scale reduces adhesive wear.
Relative to the baseline, a chromium-enriched FeNiCrCoCu coating will form a more adherent oxide film at elevated temperatures.
Relative to the baseline, the modified coating will have lower wear-volume loss at elevated temperatures.
Relative to the baseline, the modified coating will have a lower coefficient of friction at elevated temperatures.
The lower-chromium baseline will form less stable oxide films and exhibit higher wear rates.
Excessively high loads or temperatures beyond the coating's protective oxidation regime can disrupt oxide-film coverage and stability.
Disruption of oxide-film coverage and stability diminishes its protective effect.
